title: The Servo's Pulse
description: One HIGH/LOW signal, timed precisely, is all a servo needs to hear an angle. Here's exactly how a pulse becomes a position.

content.value: A Different Use for a Familiar Signal

You already know a GPIO pin only speaks HIGH and LOW, from Module 4. A servo doesn't need anything richer than that — it just cares about one specific detail of the HIGH pulse: exactly how long it lasts.

pulse width      commanded angle
1.0 ms       -->  0°
1.5 ms       -->  90°
2.0 ms       -->  180°

(repeated roughly every 20 ms, about 50 times a second)

That's the entire protocol: send a HIGH pulse somewhere between 1 and 2 milliseconds long, roughly every 20 milliseconds, and the servo's internal circuit measures the pulse's width and converts it directly into a target angle for its feedback loop to chase.

content.title: 🎯 Watch the pulse width change
content.hint: Same widget as last lesson — this time watch the pulse-width readout as you drag the angle. 1.0ms and 2.0ms are the two ends of the range.

content.value: The mapping works exactly the same read forwards or backwards: a shorter pulse always means a smaller angle, a longer pulse always means a bigger one, in a straight line between the two ends. Knowing the pulse width tells you the angle; knowing the angle tells you exactly what pulse width to send.

This is why a servo needs its own dedicated signal wire, separate from power and ground — three wires total: power, ground, and this timed pulse. You'll see all three when you wire one onto ARIA's chassis.
Key takeaway: a servo reads angle purely from how long a repeating HIGH pulse lasts, somewhere between about 1ms (0°) and 2ms (180°), sent roughly 50 times a second.

quiz.question: A servo receives a 1.5 ms HIGH pulse. Roughly what angle is it being commanded to?
quiz.explain: 1.5 ms sits exactly halfway between the 1.0 ms (0°) and 2.0 ms (180°) ends of the range — the midpoint angle.

quiz.question: What does a servo's control signal actually measure to determine the commanded angle?
options: The voltage level of the pulse
How long the HIGH pulse lasts
quiz.explain: It's purely about timing — the pulse's width, not its voltage or any other property, encodes the angle.

quiz.question: Why does a servo need three wires instead of the two a simple DC motor uses?
options: Power, ground, and a dedicated signal wire for the timed pulse
It's just tradition, two would work fine
quiz.explain: The signal pulse is a separate, precisely-timed line — mixing it with the power wires would make accurate timing unreliable.
